title: Tailoring for iterative suppliers and commercial relationships
blurb: Describe a project's context and tailor PRINCE2 for contracts, two quality systems and a supplier's iterative way of working.
question: An external supplier will build a booking app using its own iterative framework, and the customer and supplier each have their own quality system. How might the project manager tailor PRINCE2?

teach.h: Projects never sit in a vacuum
teach.body: Formally, PRINCE2 assumes no particular organizational context. A typical project involves users who specify the products they need, suppliers who provide resources and expertise, and business decision-makers who make sure the investment is and stays justified. A project may stand alone or sit within a programme or portfolio. In plain English, before tailoring, look at who is involved, who is paying whom, and what bigger structure the project belongs to.

children.label: In a portfolio
children.sub: Part of the organization's wider investment

teach.caption: Programme context is one of the influences that can lead a project to tailor the method.

teach.body: Where there is a customer-supplier relationship, often under a contract, each side brings its own way of working. The supplier has its own business case for taking part. The project may need to align its processes, practices and documents with two or more quality or management systems. The commercial management approach in the PID covers market engagement, procurement and contract management, including who is responsible and which work suppliers deliver.

teach.caption: Tailoring aligns the two so the project runs as one. The executive owns the project's business case.

teach.h: Delivery models: who does the work?

bands.label: Suppliers do most work, including much of the PM
Work shared between business and suppliers
The business does most of the work itself

teach.caption: The delivery model, part of the commercial management approach, records which parts of the work external suppliers deliver.

teach.h: A supplier with its own iterative framework
teach.body: A supplier may want to use its in-house product development framework, based on an iterative-incremental delivery method with agile approaches. To avoid confusion, the project manager might propose adding a coach to help the teams work effectively with PRINCE2 and the supplier's method together. Quality activities are tailored to suit the delivery approach, and terms can be aligned so that everyone understands the same words.

Brightwell Leisure Trust hires Tidewave Digital to build a class-booking app. Tidewave works in two-week iterations under its own quality system. Project manager Hannah Price aligns the project's quality records with both quality systems, adds an agile coach, and maps Tidewave's terms to PRINCE2's. Board members are spread across three sites, so highlight reporting is done virtually. Tidewave's director, Kofi Asante, sits on the board as senior supplier.

teach.text: Adding a coach tailors the roles; it does not replace the project manager or the board, and the PM role is still not shared. Likewise the supplier's business case explains why the supplier takes part; it never replaces the customer's business case, which the executive owns.

items: Context: standalone, within a programme or within a portfolio; users, suppliers and business decision-makers.
Commercial relationship: the supplier has its own business case; align with two or more quality systems.
Commercial management approach: market engagement, procurement, contract management; delivery model from thin to thick client.
Iterative supplier: consider adding a coach and fitting quality activities to the delivery approach.
Reporting can be adjusted, for example virtual highlight reporting for a dispersed board.

summary: You can now describe a project's context (standalone, programme or portfolio, with users, suppliers and business decision-makers) and explain how PRINCE2 is tailored for a commercial relationship. You can also say how a project adapts to a supplier's iterative framework, for example by adding a coach and aligning quality activities and reporting.

A.q: A supplier will use its own iterative-incremental framework with agile approaches. Which tailoring might the project manager propose to avoid confusion?
options: Add a coach to guide teams across both methods
Let the supplier's team lead act as executive
Drop stages so that the iterations run freely
Share the PM role with the supplier's lead
A.why: Adding a coach to help teams combine PRINCE2 with the supplier's agile method is a recognized way of tailoring roles (2.7).

whyNot.1: The executive represents the business interest and owns the business case; a supplier's team lead is not suited to it.
whyNot.2: Manage by stages is a principle; the project still needs stages as decision points.
whyNot.3: The project manager role should not be shared.

A.q: Which statement about a commercial customer-supplier relationship is correct?
options: The contract replaces the customer's business case
The supplier's board takes over directing the project
The supplier's quality system replaces the customer's
The supplier may have its own business case
A.why: In a commercial context, suppliers have their own business case for taking part in the project (1.5).

whyNot.0: The customer's business case still justifies the project; the executive owns it.
whyNot.1: The project board, including the senior supplier, directs the project.
whyNot.2: The project may need to align with two or more quality systems rather than replace one.

A.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. A project may be standalone, or part of a [?] or portfolio.
options: work package
stage plan
programme
release
A.why: A project may be standalone or sit within a programme or a portfolio (1.5, fig 1.2).

whyNot.0: A work package is a unit of work inside a project, not its wider context.
whyNot.1: A stage plan covers one stage of the project; it is part of the project, not its context.
whyNot.3: 'Release' is not one of the contexts PRINCE2 describes for a project.

B.q: The project board members work in three different countries. Which tailoring fits this?
options: Replace highlight reports with end stage reports
Provide highlight reports through virtual meetings
Ask the senior supplier to act for the whole board
Move all board decisions to the project manager
B.why: Changing the format of reports and reviews, such as virtual highlight reporting for a dispersed board, is tailoring the project controls (2.7).

whyNot.0: End stage reports come at stage ends; the board still needs time-driven highlight reports during the stage.
whyNot.2: Each board role represents a different interest; one member cannot act for the whole board.
whyNot.3: The board's decisions cannot be handed to the project manager; that would remove the directing level.

B.q:
Which two are appropriate ways to tailor PRINCE2 for a commercial customer-supplier project?
1. Aligning processes and documents with both organizations' quality systems.
2. Defining contract management responsibilities in the commercial management approach.
3. Replacing the executive with the supplier's account manager.
4. Removing the senior user because the contract fixes the requirements.
options: 1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
1 and 2
B.why: A commercial relationship may need alignment with two or more quality systems, and the commercial management approach covers contract management (2.7, 6.3.2).

whyNot.0: Statement 3 is false: the executive represents the business and owns the business case.
whyNot.1: Statement 4 is false: the senior user represents users and specifies benefits whatever the contract says.
whyNot.2: Both are false: each removes or misplaces a key board role.

B.q: Which delivery model describes suppliers doing most of the work, including much of the project management?
options: Thick client
Thin client
Hybrid
Linear-sequential
B.why: In a thin client model most of the work, including much of the project management, is done by suppliers (6.3.2.1).

whyNot.0: Thick client is the opposite end: the business does most of the work itself.
whyNot.2: Hybrid is a delivery approach mixing linear and iterative working, not a delivery model.
whyNot.3: Linear-sequential is a delivery approach, not a model of who does the work.

C.q: A customer and a supplier each have their own quality system. The project aligns its processes and documents with both. Which principle is being applied, and what is being tailored?
options: Tailor to suit the project; processes and products
Focus on products; the product quality specifications
Define roles; the senior supplier's role
Learn from experience; the lessons log
C.why: Aligning processes, practices and documents with two or more quality systems is tailoring under the 'tailor to suit the project' principle (2.7).

whyNot.1: Focus on products concerns defining products and their quality criteria, not aligning two systems.
whyNot.2: No role is changing; the change is to processes and documents.
whyNot.3: Nothing here involves recording or applying lessons.

C.q: On a project using an iterative-incremental delivery method, which tailoring of the quality practice fits?
options: Fixing every acceptance criterion before initiation
Requiring quality activities that suit the approach
Removing quality criteria from product descriptions
Moving quality assurance into the project team
C.why: The quality practice applies tailoring by requiring the quality activities appropriate to the delivery approach and product characteristics (8.7, tab 8.3).

whyNot.0: In iterative-incremental delivery, quality and acceptance criteria are refined alongside development.
whyNot.2: Products still need quality criteria; focus on products is a principle.
whyNot.3: Quality assurance is managed independently of the project management team.

C.q: A coach is added to help teams combine PRINCE2 with a supplier's agile method. Which statement is correct?
options: The coach replaces the PM, who becomes a team manager
The coach takes over project assurance for the supplier
The coach is an added role; the PM role is not shared
The coach is a new principle for agile projects
C.why: Adding a coach is tailoring of roles. The project manager role still has a single holder and should not be shared (2.7, 6.2.4).

whyNot.0: Adding a role does not remove the project manager; the PM still runs the project day to day.
whyNot.1: Project assurance stays with the board members, who decide how it is carried out.
whyNot.3: The seven principles are fixed; a coach is a role, not a principle.

reteach.title: Two organizations, one project
reteach.question: When a customer and a supplier work on the same project, what does each bring, and what must they share?

blocks.h: Bring your own, agree the shared
blocks.body: Each side brings its own business case, quality system and way of working. Tailoring decides how they fit together: shared terms, aligned quality records, an agreed reporting rhythm, perhaps a coach to bridge PRINCE2 and the supplier's agile method. The agreed fit is recorded in the PID.

blocks.text: A supplier's way of working is tailored around, not obeyed instead of PRINCE2. Stages, the board and all seven principles stay in place.

explain.body: Users specify the products, suppliers provide resources and expertise, and business decision-makers keep the investment justified. A project may be standalone or within a programme or portfolio.

test.q: Which party in a project's context makes sure the investment is and remains justified?
options: Business decision-makers
The users of the products
The external suppliers
The project team members
test.why: Business decision-makers ensure the investment is, and remains, justified (1.5).

whyNot.1: Users specify the products they need.
whyNot.2: Suppliers provide the resources and expertise.
whyNot.3: Team members build the products; they are not the party that justifies the investment.

explain.body: A customer-supplier relationship may mean aligning with two or more management or quality systems. The commercial management approach covers market engagement, procurement and contract management.

test.q: Why might a project with a commercial customer-supplier relationship need extra tailoring?
options: Its suppliers are not represented on the board
Its contract removes the need for a business case
Its principles are set by the supplier's contract
It may need to align with two or more systems
test.why: The project may need to align its processes, practices and documents with two or more quality or management systems (2.7).

whyNot.0: Supplier interests are represented on the board by the senior supplier.
whyNot.1: The customer's business case still justifies the project.
whyNot.2: Principles are fixed by PRINCE2 and cannot be set by a contract.

explain.body: Where a supplier uses its own iterative-incremental framework, the PM might add a coach to help teams work across both methods, and fit quality activities to the delivery approach.

test.q: Adding a coach on a project that uses a supplier's agile method is tailoring which element?
options: The principles
The project mandate
The roles
The business layer
test.why: Roles can be combined, split or added; adding a coach is tailoring the roles (2.7).

whyNot.1: The mandate is the business layer's trigger for the project; it is not tailored by adding roles.
whyNot.3: The business layer sits outside the project and is not one of the elements tailored.

explain.body: Report format and frequency are tailored to the context, for example virtual highlight reporting for a board spread across sites. The project manager confirms the reporting format and frequency with the board.

test.q: With whom does the project manager confirm the format and frequency of reporting?
options: The team managers
The project board
Project support
The business layer
test.why: The project manager's reporting format and frequency are confirmed with the project board (11.2.1).

whyNot.0: Team managers report to the PM through checkpoint reports; they do not set the PM's reporting.
whyNot.2: Project support helps produce reports but does not agree how the PM reports.
whyNot.3: The business layer agrees reporting with the project board, not directly with the project manager.
